orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s summary-judgment motion dismissing complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on an oily patch in defendant’s shopping-mall parking lot on April 24, 2019. She testified she had seen the patch when entering about an hour before her fall on leaving.

legal_issues.finding: Court rejected contention that oily substance was merely incidental to use of parking premises.
Plaintiff described prior sighting about an hour earlier; manager offered only general practices. Defendant failed to establish lack of constructive notice.
Obviousness did not warrant dismissal; it raised a factual issue of comparative negligence.
Open and obvious oil raised a triable comparative-negligence issue, without allocating fault.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff’s deposition described observing oil about an hour earlier.
Property manager testified only to general cleaning/inspection procedures.

quality.notes: Mall parking lot and property-manager cleaning operations support private control. Unspecified oily substance coded other; no source inferred. Prior sighting supports duration issue, not actual notice to defendant. No customer status inferred merely from entering mall.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.
On April 24, 2019, the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on an oily substance on the ground of the exterior parking lot of the defendant's shopping mall.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (Sam D. Walker, J.), dated December 22, 2021. The order granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant failed to establish, prima facie, that it did not have constructive notice of the condition that allegedly caused the plaintiff to fall ( see Skerrett v LIC Site B2 Owner, LLC , 199 AD3d at 958; Bruni v Macy's Corporate Servs., Inc. , 134 AD3d at 871; Mignogna v 7- [*2] Eleven, Inc. , 76 AD3d 1054 , 1055 [2010]; Backer v Central Parking Sys. , 292 AD2d 408, 409 [2002]). The plaintiff testified at her deposition that she saw the oily patch on the ground of the parking lot on her way into the shopping mall, approximately an hour before she slipped and fell after exiting the mall. The defendant's property manager only testified about the defendant's general cleaning and inspection procedures.
The defendant's contention that the presence of the oily substance on the ground of the parking lot was incidental to the use of the premises is without merit
Contrary to the defendant's contention, the fact that the oily substance was open and obvious only raised a triable issue of fact as to the issue of the plaintiff's comparative negligence
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Brickman’s limited appeal from July 31, 2014 order.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied dismissal of complaint and all cross claims against Brickman.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on ice in a parking lot on CLK-HP 225 Rabro’s property. Brickman provided snow removal services under an agreement to which plaintiff was not a party.

legal_issues.finding: Brickman established no duty to noncontracting plaintiff; unpleaded Espinal exceptions need not be affirmatively negated, and opposition raised no exception issue.
Plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue that Brickman launched a force or instrument of harm; no identified snow-removal mechanism was found negligent.
Plaintiff failed to raise an issue under any Espinal exception: launching harm, detrimental reliance or complete displacement of owner’s duty.
Because pleadings alleged no facts supporting an Espinal exception, Brickman’s initial burden did not require affirmatively negating each exception.
Cross claims also dismissed: owner’s potential liability would be direct, no independent tort duty shown for contribution, and no triable contract breach shown for contractual indemnity.

evidence_discussed.description: Snow-removal agreement defined contractor obligations; plaintiff was not a party. Specific contract terms not reproduced.

quality.notes: Direct plaintiff negligence duty decided alongside contribution/indemnity: not third-party-only. Whole appealed portion reversed despite different claim types. No particular plowing act, storm, actual owner fault or contract breach conclusively established.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with one bill of costs, and the motion of the defendant Brickman Group Ltd., LLC, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and all cross claims insofar as asserted against it is granted.

The plaintiff allegedly sustained personal injuries when she slipped and fell on ice in the parking lot of premises owned by the defendant CLK-HP 225 Rabro, LLC (hereinafter the owner). Thereafter, the plaintiff commenced this action against the owner and the defendant Brickman Group Ltd., LLC (hereinafter Brickman), which provided snow removal services at the premises.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant Brickman Group Ltd., LLC, appeals from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Molia, J.), dated July 31, 2014, as denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and all cross claims insofar as asserted against it.

Brickman made a prima facie showing of its entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against it by submitting evidence that the plaintiff was not a party to its snow removal agreement, and that it thus owed her no duty of care
Inasmuch as the plaintiff did not allege facts in the complaint or bill of particulars that would establish the possible applicability of any of the Espinal exceptions
Brickman was not required to affirmatively demonstrate that these exceptions did not apply in order to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law

In opposition to Brickman's prima facie showing, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether Brickman launched a force or instrument of harm, whether she detrimentally relied on the continued performance of Brickman's duties, or whether Brickman entirely displaced the owner's duty to maintain the premises in a safe condition

Brickman established, prima facie, that it was entitled to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the cross claim seeking common-law indemnification by demonstrating that the owner's liability, if any, would be based on the owner's actual wrong doing and not on vicarious liability for the Brickman's conduct

Furthermore, in opposition to the prima facie showing by Brickman that it was entitled to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the cross claims seeking contribution, the owner failed to demonstrate that Brickman owed a duty of reasonable care to the plaintiff or a duty of reasonable care independent of its contractual obligations to the owner

Finally, in opposition to the prima facie showing by Brickman that it was entitled to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the cross claim seeking contractual indemnification, the owner failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether Brickman breached the snow removal contract by failing to perform one or more of the services for which it was retained

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.
The plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on a squashed piece of fruit on the floor of the produce aisle of the defendant's store located in Yonkers.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Westchester County (O. Bellantoni, J.), entered July 11, 2013, which granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the evidence submitted in support of the defendant's motion failed to [*2] demonstrate that it lacked constructive notice of the condition alleged.

In support of the defendant's motion, the defendant relied upon, inter alia, the deposition testimony and an affidavit of an assistant manager, who worked on the night of the accident, that merely referred to general cleaning practices of the defendant and provided no evidence regarding any specific cleaning or inspection of the area in question on the day of the plaintiff's fall

The defendant's failure to establish its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law required the denial of its motion, regardless of the sufficiency of the plaintiff's papers in opposition
